# Methods

This chapter describes the experimental design of the thesis. Every tabular foundation model in the experiments is evaluated frozen. The pretrained weights are used exactly as published, and no fine-tuning or any other gradient update is applied [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning]. The only element that varies is test-time context construction, meaning which labelled training rows fill the context window and at what class ratio. As @sec-bg-pfn established, the context is the only task-specific information the model conditions on, so the context is the natural point of intervention.

The research questions of @sec-intro-rqs decompose into pairwise contrasts between the four context-construction conditions C1 to C4. The step from C1 to C2 isolates the effect of the in-context fraud ratio (RQ2). The step from C1 to C3 varies the relevance of the context (RQ3). The step from C3 to C4 adds ratio control on top of retrieval, and the comparison of C4 against C2 answers whether retrieval adds anything beyond plain rebalancing (RQ4). The comparison between best performing experimental conditions and GBDTs will answer the feasibility of these models working with extremely imbalanced datasets (RQ1). This decomposition is the spine of the design. The rest of the chapter defines the conditions and the machinery that runs them.

## Experimental conditions {#sec-methods-conditions}

Condition 1 (random) fills the context with a uniform random subsample of the training set, drawn up to the model's context limit. The fraud ratio of the context thus follows the natural prevalence of the data. This is the standard practice whose cost @sec-context-waste quantified, and it serves as the baseline for every other condition.

Condition 2 (stratified) balances the context toward a 50/50 class split. All available fraud rows enter the context, capped at half of the window, and the remaining slots are filled with randomly drawn legitimate rows. On datasets whose training split holds fewer fraud rows than half the window, the realised ratio therefore stays below 50/50. <!-- TODO: adding a inline r that fetches the real fraud ratios. And list them then here. --> Both classes are still drawn at random, so the contrast between C2 and C1 gives the effect of rebalancing the classes while relevance is held fixed.

Condition 3 (kNN control) fills the context by kNN retrieval around clusters of the scored test transactions, without touching the class ratio (@sec-methods-rap). The realised fraud share is therefore not fixed but fluctuates with the local neighbourhood of each cluster. <!-- TODO: adding a inline r that fetches the real fraud ratios from different runs. And list them then here. --> The contrast between C3 and C1 consequently varies relevance without holding the ratio fixed. Relevance is isolated cleanly only by the ratio-matched ablation described later in this chapter (@sec-methods-relevance-ablation). The unmatched form is kept deliberately, because it asks a question of its own. Does a TFM need to see fraudulent transactions from far regions of the feature space, or is the relevant region alone enough?

Condition C4 is the full RAP configuration. Retrieval becomes stratified, with a separate kNN retriever per class, so that relevant observations are drawn from both classes. On top of this, the fraud ratio of the context is enforced and swept over 5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 30 % and 50 %. When the unique fraud rows near a cluster run out before the quota is filled, fraud rows are duplicated by sampling with replacement. This oversampling is part of the method rather than a fallback. The duplication this policy introduces is quantified independently of retrieval by the sweep of @sec-methods-c2-sweep, and the ablation of @sec-methods-relevance-ablation adds a natural-ratio retrieval arm so the selection mechanism is also tested without ratio enforcement. The step from C3 to C4 is thus not just a single-factor change, it both enforces the ratio and swaps mixed retrieval for stratified retrieval. The sweep within C4 in turn isolates ratio tuning on a fixed retrieval mechanism.

The GBDT baselines run under C1 only and are trained on the full training set. The context limit is an inherent property of TFMs, so the most informative comparison for RQ1 is the full-data GBDT against the context-limited TFM. The context budget is 10,000 rows for TabPFN v2, the hard limit of its checkpoint. The remaining models run at a budget of roughly 50,000 rows. This figure is a design choice made for cross-model comparability, not the maximum of every checkpoint. <!-- TODO: future abblation to test all models at their best condition with the biggest context windows possible -->

## The Retrieval Augmented Prediction pipeline {#sec-methods-rap}

@fig-rap-overview gives an overview of the pipeline. Retrieval operates per group of test transactions rather than per test batch. The scored test set is clustered with k-means, and the number of groups $G$ is chosen by the silhouette score over $k = 2$ to $20$, computed on a seeded subsample of roughly 5,000 test rows. The chosen $G$ and its silhouette score are recorded with every run as `n_groups` and `group_silhouette`.

The motivation for this granularity is context reuse, not the number of model fits. The expensive operation in TFM inference is encoding the roughly 50,000-row context, a cost paid inside every prediction pass whenever the encoded context is not cached. Building one context per group caps the number of distinct contexts at $G$, which makes caching of the encoded context (the transformer's key-value cache) possible and would translate into significant prediction speedups in a production setting. A finer granularity, such as one context per test batch, would trade away exactly this reusability for tighter locality; per-batch retrieval is left for future research.

The retriever itself, shown in @fig-rap-overview, is a brute-force nearest-neighbour search over the training features, standardised with a scaler fit on the training split only. Cosine distance is the default metric, and the retrieval depth is derived from the context size, usually 50,000 rows. Under C3 the retrieval is mixed: the nearest training rows enter the context regardless of class, with a guard that injects the globally nearest fraud or legitimate row when a group's context would otherwise contain a single class. Under C4 the retrieval is class-conditional, with a separate retriever per class, and the fraud quota is filled by sampling with replacement when the pool of unique fraud rows near a group runs out, the oversampling policy already defined in @sec-methods-conditions. Both retrieval conditions run only on TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2, the two best-performing models under C1 and C2.

## The fraud-ratio and context-size sweep {#sec-methods-c2-sweep}

Condition C2 fixes a single balancing target, but the choice of operating point matters as much as the mechanism itself. This sweep maps the stratified-random mechanism over the full plane of fraud ratio and context size, so the ratio effect can be characterised as a curve rather than read off a single point. It also gives the C4 ratio sweep (@sec-methods-conditions) a like-for-like counterpart at every ratio: one condition with retrieval, one without, both under the same with-replacement fraud policy.

The sweep crosses nine fraud ratios (2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 20, 30 and 40 percent) with five requested context sizes (10,000, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000 and 50,000 rows). The effective context size is capped at the smaller of the training-set size and the model's checkpoint limit, and both the requested and the effective size are recorded. Two TFMs (TabICLv2 and TabPFN v3) are run on three datasets (EU CC, BankSim and PaySim), each at three seeds, with the same ensemble size (n_estimators = 4) as the main grid, for 810 runs in total. Each cell fits a single global context and one model refit; there is no per-group retrieval or refitting here, unlike C3/C4. These three datasets span the fraud-scarcity range of the formal grid: EU CC holds only about 394 training fraud rows, while BankSim and PaySim hold thousands of them, a difference that matters for the next point.

The context's fraud quota is filled by sampling with replacement once unique training fraud rows run out, the same policy used by the C4 sampler. This has two consequences. First, the requested ratio is always realised, so a high-ratio cell measures the intended ratio rather than a silently smaller one produced by exhausting the available fraud rows. Second, duplication becomes an observable and recorded quantity, the ratio of fraud rows in the context to unique fraud rows among them. On EU CC the arithmetic forces heavy duplication at high ratios: a 40 percent quota of a 50,000-row context is 20,000 fraud rows drawn against roughly 394 unique frauds, close to 50-fold duplication. BankSim and PaySim, by contrast, stay near a duplication factor of one through the low and mid ratios and reach only roughly three-to-3.5-fold at the highest ratios (about 3.5-fold on BankSim's ~5,760 training frauds and 3-fold on PaySim's ~6,570), an order of magnitude milder than EU CC's roughly 50-fold. The sweep therefore doubles as a duplication study conducted entirely in a random context. Any effect of duplication alone appears here, free of retrieval, which gives the later analysis of C4 behaviour a control that separates duplication effects from retrieval effects. <!-- TODO: crossref the results-chapter sweep section once it exists -->

## Ratio-matched relevance ablation {#sec-methods-relevance-ablation}

Neither grid contrast isolates relevance cleanly. The step from C1 to C3 varies the selection mechanism but lets the realised fraud ratio drift with the local neighbourhood of each cluster, so a ratio effect and a relevance effect are entangled. The step from C3 to C4 changes ratio enforcement and the retrieval mode at the same time, so it is not a single-factor comparison either. The ablation described here removes both confounds by crossing the two selection mechanisms independently, at a matched ratio, context size and granularity.

The design is a 2x2 over selection mechanisms: legitimate rows drawn either at random or by kNN, crossed with fraud rows drawn either at random or by kNN. This yields four arms: RR (random legitimate rows, random fraud rows), KR (kNN legitimate rows, random fraud rows), RK (random legitimate rows, kNN fraud rows) and KK (kNN both). All four arms run per group at a fixed granularity of G = 32 k-means clusters of the scored test set. Granularity is fixed rather than silhouette-selected here, so grouping is held constant across arms and cannot itself explain a difference between them. Retrieval uses the cosine metric, the requested context size is 50,000 rows, and the fraud ratio is swept over 5 percent and 10 percent, filled with the same with-replacement top-up policy as C2 and C4. The ablation runs on TabICLv2 and TabPFN v3, on EU CC, BankSim and PaySim, at three seeds. RR reproduces C2's stratified-random selection, operated at a set ratio rather than the 50/50 target and with the same with-replacement policy as the sweep, under per-group refitting, and KK is the class-conditional retrieval core of C4; each single-letter flip from one of these arms isolates one selector. Because RR runs at the same G = 32 as the other three arms, comparing it against the global-context sweep of @sec-methods-c2-sweep additionally isolates the effect of per-group granularity itself, separately from the effect of any selector.

The ablation is additionally run at a natural ratio level, defined per dataset as the training-split fraud prevalence, for the RR and KK arms only. This supplies the clean form of the C1-to-C3 contrast: both arms see the same natural class ratio and the same grouping, so only the selection mechanism differs between them. At the natural level the fraud quota sits below the unique fraud count by construction, so no duplication occurs. <!-- TODO: inline R for the realised natural ratios per dataset -->

Each contrast in this design answers a distinct question. The ratio effect is addressed in @sec-methods-conditions. Granularity is addressed by RR against the global sweep of @sec-methods-c2-sweep. Legitimate-selector relevance is addressed by RK against KK and by RR against KR. Fraud-selector relevance is addressed by RR against RK and by KR against KK. The selection mechanism at natural prevalence, free of ratio enforcement, is addressed by RR against KK at the natural level.

## Models {#sec-methods-models}

The experiments evaluate five TFMs: TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabPFN 2.6, TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2 [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs2026tabpfn26_model_card; @grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report; @qu2026tabiclv2]. TabPFN v2 runs at a context budget of 10,000 rows and TabICLv2 at roughly 48,000 rows; TabPFN 2.5, 2.6 and v3 run at a budget of roughly 50,000 rows. As stated in @sec-methods-conditions, the 50,000-row figure is a design choice for cross-model comparability, not a hard limit of every checkpoint. The installed TabPFN v3 checkpoint accepts up to 1,000,000 context rows and TabPFN 2.6 up to 100,000, both verified from the inference configuration of the `tabpfn` library version 8.0.8 used throughout, while TabPFN v2 (10,000) and TabPFN 2.5 (50,000) run at their checkpoints' own caps. All models run on a single consumer GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5070), and the library version is recorded with every run, so no reported result silently mixes library versions. <!-- TODO: add a mention to the SOTA comparison between the best case and sota -->

The GBDT baselines are XGBoost and CatBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting; @dorogush2018catboost]. Both are class-weighted, with the positive-class weight (`scale_pos_weight`) set from the training labels, and run with fixed strong defaults rather than library defaults: 2,000 trees, depth 6, learning rate 0.05, row and column subsampling of 0.8, and early stopping on PR-AUC with a patience of 50 rounds on a 10 % stratified validation split. Neither the GBDTs nor the TFMs are tuned per dataset, so the comparison is a zero-shot TFM against a fixed-default GBDT; comparisons against per-dataset tuned models are taken from the literature instead.

## Splitting protocol {#sec-methods-splits}

Each dataset is split into training and test sets with a seeded stratified 80/20 split. Banksim is instead split by its `customer` column, with every customer assigned wholly to one side of the split, because the encoded customer identifier would otherwise act as an entity key that leaks labels from training to test [@lopezrojas2014banksim]. Fifar uses its fixed published split and consequently runs at a single seed, since the seed has no effect on a fixed split.

The time columns are deliberately kept as features (`Time` in eu_cc, `step` in banksim and paysim). Under a random split this is a temporal-leakage threat: the temporal regularities shown in @fig-fraud-rate-time are available to every model and may inflate the ranking metrics of the separable datasets, paysim and eu_cc in particular. The threat is treated as a limitation in the discussion and bounded by a separate temporal-generalisation ablation outside the main grid, which splits baf by its `month` column following the dataset's published protocol [@jesus2022baf_arxiv] (@sec-app-second).
